The Crest Travels

On October 6 the S&P 500 closed at a record for the first time since August, with the typical stock 5.9% below where it stood at the last one. Then the rest got a turn. Five shared crests in seven sessions moved through the market in order, from the AI-hardware leaders to the utilities and the railroads. The ten largest companies share one phase and are descending in step. The field underneath them has no single phase. It is a rotation, measured. It is not yet a repair.

Where we left off · two weeks, one vacation, one feed incident

Sunday, Sep 27
The Room and the Rest. The index was 0.7% below its record and the typical stock 6.1% below it, the widest gap in 818 sessions. Twenty-two sessions had passed without a shared crest. A room of seventy AI-hardware stocks had carried the index. The fork was catch-up (the typical stock climbs to meet the index) against catch-down (the index takes the slide its stocks already took), graded even. A ten-session test was registered on the room.
Thursday, Oct 1
A notebook entry on singular funnels. It found that the fast counter — the closure ledger and the depth of the float — read the March slide six sessions before price while the slow maps read nothing, and that this silence was the only one of its length in the record that had not locked into one phase. It also counted the precedent for a long silence that cost nothing: thirteen cases, eleven benign over the next three months, two that paid.
Oct 2 → Oct 11
The feed dropped 66 names, Apple among them, on the morning of October 5. The package for October 2 was built on 682 names and is kept as contaminated testimony. No package exists for October 5–8. The fetch was guarded on October 11 and the record rebuilt from October 9. Everything here uses that rebuild: the five crests in this read were all seen in reconstruction, none on its own morning.
This morning
Sol read first (The Rest Gets a Turn: broader participation, a rotation of leadership, repair in progress with unfinished damage). Jason walked the board and named the deep rust, the jumpy short memory, the void in the dial's descending quarter, the sign change in the memory book. This edition is the third read, from the data, and it grades the last one.

Chapter 1 · August 13 → October 12

A record without the rest

On Tuesday, October 6 the S&P 500 closed at 7,818.93, above the August 13 record for the first time in 37 sessions. The typical stock that day was 5.9% below where it had stood at the August record, and only 27% of the 501 companies were higher. Since 2000 the index has made 35 new highs after a gap of twenty sessions or more. This is the most lopsided of them. The only other one with the typical stock down more than 3% is August 18, 2020, the COVID recovery high, at −3.2% with 44% of names higher.

The two weeks split cleanly in half. From October 1 to October 6 the index rose 1.99% and the typical stock 1.41%, with 74% of names up: the leaders' crest, the record. From October 6 to October 12 the index slipped 0.15% while the typical stock rose 0.87% and 62% of names rose: the rest's turn. Monday is the clearest example. The index closed down 0.06%; 64% of stocks rose. Add it up from September 30 and the typical stock is +2.42% against +2.03% for the index, with 73% of names up. Add it up from August 13 and the typical stock is still −5.44%, with 70% of names lower.

Who carried it, and who caught down

By sector since September 25, the catch-up came from the places September had punished. Energy's median stock rose 7.1% (86% of them up) with oil; utilities rose 4.8%, 30 of 31 up; consumer staples 2.1%. Technology's median rose 1.5%, but the sector's value-weighted contribution was 0.12 points of the index's 0.89, because inside it the old leaders fell hard: Micron −8.6%, Seagate −17.8%, Sandisk −16.3%, Intel −17.6%, Western Digital −15.3%, Qualcomm −13.6%. The ten largest companies, 39% of the index, supplied 0.47 of the 0.89 points; the other 491 supplied 0.42. Microsoft (+4.8%), Amazon (+3.9%) and Alphabet (+2.6%) did the lifting at the top; Nvidia and Apple were flat, Meta −1.2%.

The news beside it

The instrument carries no outside label; the news is placed beside the geometry so the reader can see where the two coincide, never to explain it. The Fed raised rates in September, its first hike since 2023, and the week's 10-year auction drew 5.30%, the highest auction yield since 2000. Oil is up more than 60% this year amid the war involving Iran; attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz cut traffic there the week of October 5, and a hurricane shut in about 1.3 million barrels a day in the Gulf of Mexico. On October 8 semiconductors fell 3.4% on a report that OpenAI's revenue was running some $20 billion below what it had indicated and that Broadcom was arranging $50 billion of financing for it. The geometry has oil and power at the crest and the hardware core rolling over, which is the same picture in the instrument's own words.

It is getting hotter as this is written. A Houthi strike on Riyadh's airport on Saturday killed thirteen people; on Tuesday morning the Houthis declared Saudi Aramco's oil facilities legitimate targets and told their workers to leave, while the Saudi-led coalition announced an operation against Sana'a. The Houthis have named Saudi energy production as a target, and the coalition has named the Houthi capital. Jason's note from the weekend, carried here as a hypothesis beside the read: separate wars propagate through the same fuel, shipping and refining capacity without anyone coordinating them, and the equity market can broaden while the systems under the economy tighten. The instrument would see that, if it comes, as pressure returning to names that today sit quiet above the floor. CPI is Wednesday; earnings season opens with the banks.

Chapter 2 · October 2 → October 12

Five crests in seven sessions

Every stock has a short rhythm: it rises for a week or two, tops out, falls back, turns up again. The Burst Monitor tracks that rhythm for every company as a phase in a twenty-session cycle, and it logs a closure on any day when at least 8% of its pool — 59 names of 749 — reach the top of their rhythm together. Closures are ordinary: they fire on about six sessions in ten. What is rare is their absence. From August 26 through October 1 there were none, 26 sessions, while the index drifted sideways and the typical stock fell.

Then they came in a run. In today's record: October 2, 68 names at their crest against the 59 needed; October 5, 73; October 6, 72; October 9, 77; October 12, 63. All five were index up days or flat, which matters, and which chapter 4 returns to. A silence that ends on up days at a record is a different animal from the March silence, which ended on April 9, eight sessions after the March 30 low (−9.1% from the high), with the index still 2.2% below it.

The cast travels

The instrument also knows who crested. On the 501-name roster the closers on October 2 were the hardware supply chain and the AI industrials: Analog Devices, Applied Materials, Lam, KLA, Microchip, Coherent, Lumentum, Nvidia, Microsoft, Texas Instruments, Synopsys, Palantir, and Caterpillar, Emerson, Honeywell, Johnson Controls, Rockwell. Twenty-six of 47 were technology. October 5 added Alphabet and the refiners. October 6 added Tesla, the materials names and the power-equipment names. By October 9 the crest was broad: Amazon, Berkshire, Costco, Chevron, Exxon, Cisco, the insurers, a few utilities; technology was 12 of 58. On October 12 the closers were twelve utilities, the railroads, UPS, a few insurers and financials, and one technology name.

Two numbers follow the cast across the week. The closers' median return from the August high to September 25 — how far behind they had been — runs +1.4%, +1.9%, −1.1%, −0.9%, −6.3%. The closers' share of the index's value runs 20%, 27%, 9%, 28%, 3.5%. The crest went from the stocks that had led to the stocks that had lagged in seven sessions, and the lagging stocks' turn was the lightest by weight.

What the ledger showed on each morning

None of these five crests was seen on its own morning. The October 2 package was built on 682 names and showed 22 closers; there was no package at all for October 5 through 8; the first clean rebuild, on October 11, showed October 2 at 64. October 9 printed exactly at the line (59 of 59) on October 11, below it (58) on the October 12 build, and at 77 this morning. That is not noise in the data. It is the construction. The phase of each stock is read from a transform over its whole price history, and at the newest session the transform has nothing to its right. The count of names at their crest on the newest day runs low on its first print and settles upward, unevenly, as sessions are appended.

On nine of nine mornings from September 21 to October 1 the newest session printed below where it settled, by 19 names on average (median 13); one build later the mean gap was +2.8, with individual builds still off by as much as 14 either way.

Construction · the first print runs low

This is the mirror of a rule the read journal already carries for the amplitude book, whose newest print runs high (42 of 42 mornings last audit). Both come from the same transform at the same edge. Two consequences for this read. October 12's 63, four over the line, is a first print and is more likely to rise than to drop. And a morning that shows a near-miss within about twenty of the line is a morning that may already have had a closure. The next build, after Tuesday's close, is when Monday's crest becomes a fact.

The precedent for a silence that cost nothing

The October 1 notebook counted every closure silence of fifteen sessions or more since 2000: 48 of them. In 35 the index was down more than 5% at some point inside. Thirteen kept the damage inside −5%. Over the three months after those thirteen ended, eleven did nothing in particular (−1% to +10%) and two paid: June 2011 (−9.4%) and December 2024 (−11.3%). This silence is the fourteenth. It ran 26 sessions, the index was never more than 1.6% below its August 25 close inside it, and it was −0.1% when the first crest came. That is the record's lean for what follows: counts, not a probability, and the condition was written after looking at the shape.

Chapter 3 · the map, two lenses

Pressure went into the rest

The map's vertical axis is each stock's participation pressure against its own one-year normal, with the floor at normal. Above the floor is quiet; below is more than normal. Stocks move up between closures as their pressure decays with a 21-session half-life, and they dive on closure days. So the question after a release is not how many dove but who is below the floor now, and which way they are drifting sideways while they float.

On Monday, 214 of 501 names sit below the floor, 36% of the index's value, 57 of them deep. By sector it is the rest: 61% of financials (43 of 70), 52% of energy, half of materials, staples and real estate, 42% of industrials. Technology is 32% (27 of 85), healthcare 32%. The heavy names below the floor are Microsoft, Meta, Micron, Berkshire, JPMorgan, Walmart, Visa, Johnson & Johnson, Cisco, Bank of America, Costco. Three-quarters of the below-floor names moved left over the last five sessions, toward looser coupling with the market's pulse. The hardware core — Nvidia, Apple, Broadcom, AMD — is still above the floor, quiet. The release put pressure into the names that had been left behind, and not, so far, into the ones that had led.

How much of the six-month arrow is the window

The six-month lens is a 126-session rectangular window. Between October 5 and October 12 it rolled off April 7 through April 13: the days of the April 9–15 release, when nearly every name was at high pressure and tightly coupled. The last edition flagged this exit ahead of time. The measurement is simple. Compute Monday's map twice: once with the window as it is, and once with the window held where it stood on October 5 and the five new sessions appended. The difference between the two Mondays is the exit. The difference between the held-window Monday and October 5 is the new data.

Taken back to September 25, the same split says what was real in the six-month crowd's unwind. The crowd — names in band and tightly coupled — went from 157 to 7 on this lens. With the window held it would have gone to 39. So about 120 of the 150 names that left the crowd left on the data, and 30 left on the window. The crowd really did let go. The five-session arrow's coherence and about two-thirds of the coupling drop are the window.

The horizon shear, which connects each name's position on the two lenses on the same day, has fallen from R 0.68 on September 25 to 0.17: the two lenses now agree that the field is loose, and the shear vector itself is weak. It is not a second confirmation of the compass, and the compass it would confirm is mostly the exit.

Chapter 4 · the Phase Dial

Ten names in step, a field with no phase

The dial puts every stock's phase on one clock face. Home, at the top, is the crest of its twenty-session rhythm; the trough is at the bottom; the right side is descending, the left side rising. Two hands sum the roster. The count hand treats every stock equally; the weight hand weighs them by market value, as the index does. A hand's length, R, is coherence: 1 means every stock is at the same point of its cycle, 0 means they cancel. A hand shorter than 0.35 is a zero, and its direction is not a position.

What the weight hand is made of

Split the roster at the ten largest companies and the weight hand resolves into one fact. The ten — Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet (two share lines), Meta, Broadcom, Tesla, Micron — have a coherence of 0.92 among themselves by weight and 0.89 by count, at 0.18 of a cycle past the crest. The other 491 names have a weight coherence of 0.19 and a count coherence of 0.25: both zeros. The market's "firm weight hand" is the ten. Nvidia and Microsoft crested on October 5; Alphabet, Tesla and Amazon on October 9. Apple, Meta and Micron had crested before the window and never left the crest quarter until Micron did. By Monday nine of the ten were between 0.12 and 0.27 of a cycle past the crest and Micron was further along at 0.36, descending together, while the rest of the market had no phase at all.

The rest of the market, by sector

Below the ten, the dial sorts the sectors in the order the crest reached them. Energy is at the crest now (count R 0.65 at 0.02 of a cycle). Utilities (R 0.79 at 0.96) and real estate (0.68 at 0.76) are rising into it, financials (0.48 at 0.79) behind them. Technology is dispersed past it: 40 of its 85 names in the crest quarter, 15 descending, 21 at the trough, R 0.30. Industrials have no phase (R 0.12). This is the same traveling crest as chapter 2, read as a position instead of an event: the leaders have passed the top, the oil and power names are at it, the rate-sensitive names are coming up to it.

What the record says about this shape

The shape on the dial is: weight hand firm, count hand a zero, weight just past home. On today's roster, with episodes five sessions apart and the last sixty sessions excluded, the record has 43 of them. Over the next twenty sessions the index's median move was +1.5% with 63% up, against +1.3% and 64% at the base rate. The tenth-percentile outcome was −6.2% against −4.8%. The count hand went on to lock (R above 0.55) within ten sessions in 56% of the cases, against 72% at base: after this shape the field tends to stay dispersed. A tighter cut — weight above 0.40, count below 0.30 — has eleven cases, a −4.7% median, and a list of dates that includes October and December 2007, February 2009, August 2020, February 2022 and February 2025. Across a grid of 64 nearby thresholds the median outcome swings from −6.5% to +1.8%, so the tight cut is a tail note with famous dates in it, not a lean. The conditions were written after looking at the shape.

A rule for the guide · coordination is a magnitude; the tape supplies the sign

Jason's point on the board walk: the field can move together in either direction, and what price is doing as it coordinates is what tells you where "up" lives in that episode. Measured on the count hand crossing 0.55 — 259 locks since 2000 — the tape was up into 59% of them. Coordination-up is the majority case. And the sign at the lock carries forward content. Locks with the tape down into them: next-20 median +2.8%, 69% up; down more than 2%: +3.8%, 76% up; locked at the trough: +3.7%, 78% up. That is the record's bottom shape, the March shape. Locks with the tape up into them: +0.65%, 58%; up more than 2%: +0.2%, 51%; locked at home: +0.6%, 56%. That is its exhaustion shape, and on the instrument alone the two look the same.

So: a lock is not a slide. It is a field moving together, and the episode decides the direction. In this episode the field is not locking — the count hand went 0.50 → 0.24 as the crest traveled. The coordinated object is the ten heavy names, and the tape under their crest was a record. If a lock comes in the next weeks, the ten-session return into it is the number to print beside it.

Which chord — where the hand pointed when it locked

Jason's second question: there are different chords, so does it matter which one locks? Split the same 259 locks by where the count hand pointed when it crossed 0.55, and the cycle position sorts outcomes far more sharply than the tape's sign. A lock just past the crest — the field synchronized at the top of its rhythm — is the record's top shape: 109 cases, next-20 median −1.6%, 36% up, worst-in-20 median −3.7%. A lock just past the trough is its bottom shape: 51 cases, +6.1%, 84% up, and the index's low lands a median two sessions later, which is to say at the lock. The flanks are starker still. Locked on the descending flank (ψ 0.15–0.35, 31 cases): 29% up, −3.7%, tenth percentile −16.5%. Locked on the rising flank (0.65–0.85, 58 cases): 90% up, +4.1%, and the worst-in-20 median is +0.1% — the index did not look back.

On the specific hypothesis that a descending lock means a price low is coming as the field moves to the trough: half right. After the 24 descending locks the index did go lower, a median −3.1% below the lock, with the low landing eight sessions on. But the hand reached the trough in 96% of cases a median of one session later, and the price low coincided with that arrival within two sessions only 30% of the time. The phase runs ahead of price. The lock's position is a direction marker; the field's arrival at the trough does not date the low. Which hand locks matters less than where: count alone, weight alone and both are within a point of one another. These cuts overlap the tape-sign split — a crest lock has the tape up into it four times in five — so they are the better version of the same finding, not a second one, and a crest lock means every stock just rallied against its own 20-day mean, so part of the forward number is that quantity reverting. The conditions were written after seeing the shape.

What happens if everything swings

By construction the 55% of the index's value sitting just past the crest will advance into the descending quarter over the coming sessions; a phase moves. The question is whether price follows, and whether the rest of the field falls into step. After the 43 past episodes of this shape, in the 22 where the weight hand was still near home ten sessions later the index was +1.4%; in the 12 where it had rolled into descent or the trough the index was −2.9%. That is not a forecast and it cannot be one: the heavy names' phase and the index's price are one fact measured twice. What the dial can do is show the swing as a position while it happens, and show whether the count hand rises with it. A count hand above 0.55 while the ten descend is the field swinging together. A count hand that stays a zero while the laggards keep cresting is the rotation continuing.

Chapter 5 · Waves and the two books

The shorter current turned

The memory book asks, for each candidate depth of memory from a few months to six years, how well the market's shared burst energy lines up with how far the index sits below its high, and at what lead or lag. The depth with the strongest alignment is the balance point, and the instrument tracks which depth holds it. Since early September the incumbent has been the same memory, stepping from 360 to 384 sessions as it ages, about a year and a half, with a correlation of +0.878 and a control streak of 27 sessions. Positive means burst energy and drawdown depth move together at that depth. Gold on the plane.

Jason saw the sign change on the plane; it is real, and it is a different kind of change from the one the last edition was watching for. The switch is a switch of correlation peak, not a line crossing zero: at a fixed 180-session depth the correlation went from −0.76 on October 5 to +0.79 on October 6, and the selected lag jumped from −91 to −131 sessions. A negative patch remains at 132–168 sessions; the whole spectrum did not turn. The 204-session current is now 0.020 behind the incumbent in absolute correlation and has no print in the settled five-session book: handoff distance 3, which is a ceiling, not a measurement. There is no active challenger.

What would it mean if 204 took control? September's challenger was anti-coupled: a handoff to it would have flipped the sign of the market's memory. October's is coupled, like the incumbent. A handoff now would keep the sign and halve the depth — the market remembering a nearer past, in the same key. The very short end is jumpy, as Jason said: 60- and 72-session memories select leads of 20 and 24 sessions, 84 selects a lag of 43. Those are narrow patches that change peak from one build to the next, and the controlled 384 still selects a lag of 168 sessions. Sign, lag and depth are three coordinates; only the sign changed.

The amplitude book, as printed and as it settled

The second book asks whether the companies' amplitude states agree. In the fixed book, a spread below its own trailing floor is an agreement day — a locked zero, the "anchors" of the last edition — and a spread well above it is apart. Its newest print runs high and settles down, every morning. October 2 printed 1.513 and now reads 1.135, near the floor. October 9 printed 1.528 and now reads 1.217. In today's reconstruction the book came back to agreement once during the release, on October 8 (1.029 against a floor of 1.113), between the leaders' crests and the rest's; it was near the floor from September 30 to October 2, apart on October 5–7 with its peak on the day of the record, and apart again on October 9 and 12. Monday's 1.380 is a first print; on the audit's rule it is more likely to settle down toward the floor (1.11) than to stay where it printed. The signature tooth S1, which ran on one horizon from August 20, is absent at every horizon; the structural state is neutral.

Then and now

Three restatements change what the last edition could have seen. The October 2 closure was invisible on its own morning and first appeared on October 11 — condition strong, date reconstructed. The October 9 closure fired, un-fired and fired again across three builds; the first-print rule explains it. And the room's September 25 cohesion, saved as 65 of 70, is 51 in today's rebuild, so the comparable path is 51 → 44 and not a 65 → 44 exodus. A lesson for the guide from the test itself: a room's weight hand can be one name's hand; test a room by count, or by weight with its dominant member set aside.

Chapter 7 · unresolved

Rotation, or a swing

The last edition's fork was catch-up against catch-down, and the market answered it sideways: the index made its high alone and then stood still while the rest took a turn. The new fork is about the turn. Does the crest keep traveling — the laggards cresting, the field staying dispersed, the gap to August closing a point at a time — or do the ten heavy names, now descending in step, pull the field into one phase on the way down?

branch oneThe rotation continues

  • The next closure's cast is the laggards again: utilities, financials, real estate, staples, a small share of the index's value.
  • The count hand stays a zero (below 0.35) while the sector hands keep moving through the crest in order.
  • The typical stock keeps matching or beating the index on the days the index is flat; the gap to August 13 narrows from −5.4.
  • The names below the floor keep drifting left and resurface on the half-life without a new dive from the leaders.
  • The weight hand's phase advances past 0.25 with the index holding near its high: the heavies rolling over in their rhythm without the tape rolling over.

branch twoThe field swings together

  • The next closure's cast is the ten heavy names a second time, which would mean the rest never held its gain.
  • The count hand rises above 0.55 while the weight hand descends: the field falling into one phase on the way down, the March shape at a high. Print the ten-session return into the lock beside it.
  • The hardware core — still quiet above the floor — dives, and the names below the floor drift right, toward coupling.
  • The amplitude book's October 8 zero survives the next builds and is joined by another: agreement returning on the way down rather than inside the release.
  • The 204 current banks a settled print (distance 1 or 2) as the tape turns; same sign, half the depth.

The record's lean, printed as counts: 43 episodes of today's dial shape, next-20 median +1.5%, 63% up, p10 −6.2%, and the field stayed dispersed more often than not. Fourteen mild silences, eleven benign. Thirty-five gapped new highs, none this lopsided. A tight cut of eleven with famous dates in it. The condition was written after seeing the shape; survivorship weighs on everything before 2015; the newest three ticks of the chord, the closure ledger and the amplitude book restate.

    Held near home at ten sessions, or rolled past 0.25 into descent. The heavies' phase and the index's price are one fact: the dial shows it as a position while the tape shows it as a return.

  4. The next closure's castnow: Oct 12's was utilities and rails, 3.5% of the index

    Laggards again, or the leaders a second time. The ledger names them; the sector hands show them coming.

  5. The amplitude book's October 8 zeronow: reconstructed, 1.029 against 1.113 · Oct 9 and 12 are first prints

    Does it survive the next two builds, and do October 9 and 12 settle near the floor as the audit says they will. Agreement inside a release is a different thing from agreement before one.

  6. The 204 currentnow: +0.858, margin 0.020, distance 3

    A settled print at distance 1 or 2 is the first real handoff since September 4. A coupled challenger keeps the sign and halves the depth.

Three reads, one morning

The rest has begun to catch up, while several names that carried the index are giving ground. That looks like rotation and partial repair. I'd downgrade my September catch-down lean.

Sol, first pass, before the board walk

"Healthy" is too strong — I don't know that we know that. Rust up top. The tip is barely leading, bouncing around. Look at that void in the down cycle. What happens if everything swings? And we did have a sign change in a current.

Jason, the board walk

Coordinated movement doesn't mean auto crash or dip. It means coordinated — pushed in a direction. The direction of the break against price as it happens tells you where "up" lives in that episode. Everything is relative to what is happening now.

Jason, on the rule that went into the guide

A record without the rest, then a turn: a crest traveling leaders-to-laggards in seven sessions, the ten heavies descending in step, the field with no phase. Rotation, measured. Repair is when the laggards' crest holds and the gap closes, and it hasn't yet.

Glossary, in the order the piece uses it

Pressure, the floor
Each stock's participation in the market's shared bursts, measured against its own one-year normal. The floor is normal. Above it is quiet; below it, more than normal. Pressure decays with a 21-session half-life and is refilled only on closure days.
Coupling
The correlation of a stock's pressure with the whole market's burst energy over the lens's window. The map's horizontal axis. It is not the correlation of its price with the index.
Phase, the crest, home
Where a stock sits in its own twenty-session rhythm, read as an angle: 0 is the crest (home), 0.25 descending, 0.5 the trough, 0.75 rising.
Closure, release, silence
A closure fires when at least 8% of the pool (59 of 749) are at their crest on the same day. A release is a closure after a long silence. A silence is a run of sessions without one.
The count hand, the weight hand
The roster's mean phase as a vector, every stock equal (count) or weighted by today's market value (weight). R is the vector's length, 0 to 1; below 0.35 it is a zero. ψ is its direction, in cycles.
A lock
The count hand rising through 0.55: the field moving in one phase. A magnitude; the tape at that moment supplies the sign.
The lens, the window exit
Pressure and coupling are rolling 126- or 252-session measures. When a run of high-pressure days leaves the window, every name's position moves by construction.
The compass
The mean of the names' five-session displacements on the map. R is agreement on direction; drift is the mean displacement's length.
The room
A community in the Currents river: names that co-burst over a 63-session window, matched day to day. The seventy of the last edition were frozen on September 23.
The balance point, the incumbent
The depth of memory at which burst energy and drawdown depth are most aligned; the incumbent is the depth that holds it in the settled five-session book. Distance 3 means no challenger has a print.
The amplitude book, a locked zero
The spread of the names' amplitude states at the one-year rung against its own trailing floor. Below the floor is agreement, a locked zero; well above it is apart. Its newest print runs high.
First print, settled
What a series shows on the morning its newest session arrives, against what it shows after later sessions are appended. The phase-based series restate at the edge: closers low, amplitude high.
THEN / NOW
A saved morning's package (testimony) against today's rebuilt history (reconstruction). A reconstruction is never called an earlier warning.
